title: Geography as narrow-mindedness
core: All three start as literal map words — a province, a parish, an island — and all three are used on the GRE in their figurative sense: a mind whose reach stops at some boundary. The charge in every case is limited *range*, never limited intelligence; each can be leveled at someone perfectly capable inside their own patch. What separates them is which feature of the map does the metaphorical work: distance from the centre, size of the patch, or the water around it.

words.nuance: The only one that also indicts **taste** — the target is behind the times and unpolished, not merely limited. It carries a built-in hierarchy, so it can only be spoken downward from an assumed centre, which is why it makes the speaker sound snobbish in a way the others don't. Also the only one of the three that works as a noun for a person: *a provincial*.

Measures the **size of what you care about**, not your polish or your isolation. It attaches most naturally to disputes, concerns and interests — a parochial quarrel is one whose stakes evaporate a mile outside the village. No suggestion of backwardness: a parochial committee can be sophisticated and well-informed, just aimed at a trivially small target.

Points at the **barrier** rather than the smallness — sealed against outside influence, and comfortable that way; complacency is baked in. It's the standard diagnosis for a self-sufficient group that has stopped importing (a discipline, a nation, an elite institution), so unlike the other two it can describe the powerful centre rather than the periphery. Coolest and most clinical of the three.

exam_note: The exam usually keys on the literal sense you've forgotten (parish, island, non-capital) or forces a choice between them via context: "sealed off, incurious" → insular; "small-stakes, only matters locally" → parochial; "unsophisticated, behind the metropolis" → provincial.
